title: SoupBinTCP
text: Multicast is fast, but some links need a reliable, ordered stream. SoupBinTCP is Nasdaq's thin framing for exactly that: a login, sequenced data, heartbeats, and replay from any point.

title: Framing a byte stream
text: TCP delivers bytes, not messages. One read can end halfway through a packet, or hold three of them. So every Soup packet starts with a two byte length, then a one byte type. The length counts the type byte and the payload. The parser reads the length, waits for that many bytes, and only then hands the packet on.

title: Ten packet types
text: The type is one ASCII character. The client sends L to log in, U for unsequenced data, R for a heartbeat, and O to log out. The server answers A for login accepted or J for rejected. Then S for sequenced data, H for its heartbeat, and Z for end of session. A plus sign is a debug packet, ignored by both sides.

title: Login and replay
text: The login request is 49 bytes. A username of six characters, a password of ten, a session of ten, and a requested sequence number of twenty. Text fields are padded with spaces, and the number is ASCII digits, right-justified. Here, the client has processed 41,999 messages, so it asks for 42,000. The server replies Login Accepted, with sequence 42,000. Then it replays every message from there, and carries straight on with live data.

title: Counting, not stamping
text: Notice what sequenced data does not carry: a sequence number. Both sides simply count, from one at the start of each session. Gaps cannot happen on one TCP connection. So after a disconnect, you log in again with your count plus one, and nothing is lost or repeated. Ask for zero, and you start from the most recent message.

title: Heartbeats and timeouts
text: Each side sends a heartbeat after one second without sending anything else. The server drops a client that is silent for about fifteen seconds, and a connection that sends no login within about thirty. End of session means the session is over, and cannot be rejoined.

title: In the lab
text: In the lab, libs slash soup writes these packets into fixed buffers, and a stream parser reassembles them from the socket. The simulated exchange speaks OUCH orders over SoupBinTCP. On login it replays the account's messages from the requested number. And the lab's vendor feeds use it as their transport.

title: Takeaway
text: So when do you choose Soup over Mold? Soup is reliable and simple, but one slow reader or one lost segment stalls everything behind it. Mold multicast is fast, and recovery is your problem. SoupBinTCP gives you an exact, gapless copy of the session, if you can wait for it.
